newsitem.title: GERMANY: BUBA REPO TALK PERSISTS,BUT MONEY MARKET SCEPTICAL.
newsitem.headline: BUBA REPO TALK PERSISTS,BUT MONEY MARKET SCEPTICAL.

text.p: Speculation that the Bundesbank could open the door to higher short-term interest rates dominated talk in Germany's money market on Monday, helping boost borrowing rates for overnight funds.

Yet traders were increasingly sceptical that the Bundesbank would act this week to nudge its main money market rate or repo higher, with some now judging it unlikely any change would come before the policy-making council returns from a summer break.

Overnight funds were trading at 3.05/10 percent on Monday, with most dealings taking place at 3.07/08 percent, well above the so-called repo rate, which acts as an anchor for money market rates. The repo has been at three percent for a year.

Talk that this rate could be raised was first sparked by a Bundesbank decision at its council meeting on July 24 to leave its options open in the second part of its four-week summer break -- by not announcing repos for that period in advance.
This marked a change from the recent established pattern.
One option open to the central bank would be to set a second tender alongside the standard fixed interest rate repo -- the instrument it has used consistently over the last year.

This second tender could be set at variable interest rates, where banks bid for funds at rates of their choice and not just for volume allocation. This would signal that the central bank was prepared to allow rates for these funds to drift higher.

If it were to opt for this strategy, the Bundesbank could theoretically announce such a move as early as tomorrow, when it is already due to call for bids for three percent funds as announced after its last Bundesbank council meeting on July 24.

But it could also hold off for a further week -- until the current batch of pre-announced tenders have been allotted -- and either adopt the same strategy or switch over fully to a variable repo tender. Or it could simply set next week's at a higher fixed interest rate or an unchanged three percent.
While speculation lingered about a "double-decker" tender, many traders were sceptical that the Bundesbank would take the step, arguing that it was hard to see what it would achieve.

Any repo rate rise that was large enough to stop the surging dollar in its tracks could spell disaster for the domestic economy, they said, while a minimal move of a few basis points would likely be instantly discounted by markets.
"The Bundesbank will not follow a policy of tiny steps," one trader at a German bank active in the money market said. "That would have no influence on markets."
A second money market trader agreed.
"I do not think they will take any action at all," the trader said.
"For the time being I think we can forget the idea of a change...It would be a mistake to hand over control of the repo rate to the market at the moment."

Analysts at ABN AMRO were also sceptical. Under the headline, "Will it come, or won't it?" its investment research department commented that such a move could be judged as necessary to rein in the dollar, now trading above 1.87 marks.
"For this reason the Bundesbank could -- but in our view should not and will not -- raise interest rates or switch to a variable tender," ABN AMRO said.

Speculation the central bank could set a second repo at variable rates alongside a fixed rate pact was sparked by an article in the Handelsblatt newspaper last week, based on an interview with Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick.
Traders noted however that Koebnick had spoken of the possibility of raising interest rates in a European context.
"If we look at the chances of the Bank of France raising its rates it is clear that a coordinated action to tighten policy is not likely to emerge," one trader said.
If no unexpected announcement is made tomorrow, the focus of speculation will turn to August 12, the next date when a tender is due for announcement.

The outcome then -- with all of the above options open -- will be the decision of the Bundesbank's directorate, operating on the basis of policy guidelines agreed in the July 24 council meeting. The guidelines given are shrouded in secrecy.
